name: Cookie diet

lead: The cookie diet replaces most meals with specially formulated cookies designed to curb appetite, leaving a single regular meal. People use it to lose body fat quickly, which can leave the face and body looking leaner.
It was developed by Florida physician Sanford Siegal in 1975 and was sold through franchised centres in the 2000s. It is described as a fad, calorie-restricted diet.

paras: The original plan has people eat around six cookies through the day (about 500 calories) and a dinner of about 300 calories, for roughly 800 calories daily. Other versions use four to six cookies with one meal.

The plan is described as unbalanced and its calorie level as too low. Very-low-calorie diets generally carry risks of nutrient shortfall and muscle loss; anyone with a medical condition is advised to consult a clinician.

angle.text: The diet creates a large calorie deficit, which people use to cut body fat and get a leaner look in the face and body.

lead: The cookie diet is a weight-loss plan in which appetite-suppressing meal-replacement cookies stand in for most meals. It was created by South Florida physician Sanford Siegal, who in 1975 developed amino-acid cookies to reduce his patients' hunger [1].

People use it to reduce body fat, which in looksmaxxing terms is a route to a leaner face and sharper definition. Siegal's original plan had patients eat six cookies (about 500 calories) and a dinner of about 300 calories, around 800 calories daily [1].

Franchised cookie-diet centres operated from 2002 to mid-2006. Siegal's relationship with the franchise ended in August 2006, and the company that licensed his name filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on 25 September 2008 [1]. The plan is classed as a fad diet and described as unbalanced and too low in calories [1].

paras: Variants use four to six cookies a day, sometimes with one meal such as six ounces of meat [1]. The original structure is six cookies and a roughly 300-calorie dinner [1].
Siegal developed the cookies in 1975 while researching a book on natural foods and hunger. Franchised weight-loss centres ran 2002 to mid-2006, and the licensee filed for bankruptcy in 2008 [1].
The diet is described as a fad diet whose 800-calorie requirement is too low and which is unbalanced [1].

timeline.event: Siegal's link to the franchise ends; centres stop operating [1]
